newsitem.title: INDIA: India says U.S. court clears Sikh's extradition.
newsitem.headline: India says U.S. court clears Sikh's extradition.

text.p: A U.S. court has cleared the extradition to India of a suspected top Sikh militant leader wanted by New Delhi for a bus bombing and an attempted political assassination, authorities said on Tuesday.

Officials of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), India's federal police agency, said a Texas court had cleared the way for the extradition of Daya Singh Sandhu, who was arrested in Minneapolis in 1995.

Sandhu, also known as Lahoria, was believed to be one of the leaders of the Khalistan Liberation Force, a militant outfit fighting for a separate Sikh nation in the northern state of Punjab which they call Khalistan, or Land of the Pure.
Sandhu was wanted in India in several criminal cases, including a bus bombing that killed eight and injured 29.
CBI officials said he was wanted in the attempted assassination in 1994 of the then head of the Congress party's youth wing, M.S. Bitta.
He was also suspected of involvement in the abduction of the son of former government minister Ram Niwas Mirdha, as well as arms trafficking in India, authorities said.
Sandhu was arrested by the U.S. Immigration and Naturalisation Service (INS) in August 1995 at the Minneapolis-St. Paul airport and charged with illegal entry into the United States and visa fraud.
Arrested with him were his wife, Kamaljeet Kaur, and Pinder Brar, a Canadian immigrant and Indian citizen.

The arrests followed a tip from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. An INS investigation found Sandhu, his wife and son entered the United States in New York in July 1995 using false identities and counterfeit documents.
After the arrests, INS agents turned up evidence that Brar was planning to smuggle Sandhu and his family into Canada using another set of false papers.
India had sought the help of Interpol in gaining his extradition, CBI officials said.
Officials said it was not known when Sandhu would be extradited to India.
No details were immediately available from U.S. authorities.
